passage: Hrithik, put the phone down for a minute. You've been saying Aman doesn't care since morning, just because he hasn't replied. Let your Tejas Chacha tell you something. When I was fifteen, my best friend Joseph and I were meant to go to the Dussehra mela together. I waited at the bus stand two hours. He never came. I was so sure he'd found cooler friends that I didn't speak to him for a month. Walked past him in the school corridor like he was a lamp post. Then his sister told me their father had been rushed to hospital that evening, and they had no phone at home. A month, beta. I lost a month with my best friend because I decided what kind of person he was. So charge your patience before you decide about Aman.

qa.q: How long did Tejas wait at the bus stand?
qa.a: Tejas waited at the bus stand two hours.

qa.q: Why was fifteen-year-old Tejas so sure Joseph didn't care?
qa.a: Waiting two hours alone hurt, and with no other information, 'he found cooler friends' felt like the only explanation.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do before deciding Aman doesn't care?
qa.a: He could send one kind message asking if everything is okay, and keep in mind a dead phone or trouble at home.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt when Tejas ignored him in the corridor?
qa.a: Joseph was coping with his father being rushed to hospital, so being treated like a lamp post by his best friend would have hurt even more.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at fifteen, he blamed a friend's character for not turning up when a family emergency was the reason.

passage: Results were out at ten, and by noon Jahnavi had messaged Rafiq six times. "Got 91 in science!!" "Hello??" "Wow. Okay." No reply came. Rain hammered the tin roof of her tuition centre, and the power had gone twice. "He literally doesn't care," she told Pooja, stabbing her pen into the desk. "He replies to everyone else in two seconds. I'm just not important." She didn't wonder why the whole building's internet was down, or why Rafiq's mother had looked so worried at the market that morning. By evening she'd drafted a long, cold message ending the friendship. At eight, a call came from an unknown number. "Jahnavi? It's Rafiq. Phone fell in a puddle. Nani's in hospital. I saw your marks on Ammi's phone. Congratulations."

qa.q: How many times had Jahnavi messaged Rafiq by noon?
qa.a: By noon Jahnavi had messaged Rafiq six times.

qa.q: Why did 'He literally doesn't care' feel true to Jahnavi?
qa.a: She was excited about her 91 and he usually replies in two seconds, so his silence felt like a message about how little she mattered.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try before drafting a cold message?
qa.a: She could think of other reasons for the silence, like the rain, the power cuts or his worried mother, and wait to hear from him.

qa.q: What was Rafiq's day like while Jahnavi was angry?
qa.a: Rafiq had lost his phone in a puddle and his Nani was in hospital, yet he still called to congratulate her. 🙏

grounding: A teenager decides a friend doesn't care when he doesn't reply, ignoring clues of a dead phone and a family crisis.

passage: Gurleen's birthday cake sat half-eaten on the dining table of their Chandigarh flat, and she kept checking her phone. Wishes from cousins, from her tuition group, even from the aunty downstairs. Nothing from Nilesh, who lived two lanes away and had been her friend since Class 3. "Typical," she said to her mother. "He only remembers people when he needs notes." She scrolled back through old chats hunting for proof: the time he forgot to return her compass, the time he left early from her Holi party. Every memory seemed to fit. She did not think about his grandfather being unwell all month, or his phone screen being cracked for a week. At 11:40 pm, Nilesh knocked on the door, holding a crumpled card and a single laddoo.

qa.q: What was Nilesh holding when he knocked at 11:40 pm?
qa.a: Nilesh was holding a crumpled card and a single laddoo.

qa.q: Why did every old memory seem to fit for Gurleen?
qa.a: Once she decided Nilesh was selfish, she went hunting for proof, so the compass and the Holi party felt like evidence while his reasons stayed invisible.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen when a friend goes quiet on an important day?
qa.a: Pause before labelling him, remember what is happening in his life, like his unwell grandfather, and maybe ask if he's okay.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nilesh standing at the door that late?
qa.a: Nilesh may feel guilty for being so late and worried she's upset, even though he made the effort to come in person.

grounding: A teenager reads a friend's missing birthday wish as uncaring, overlooking his cracked phone and unwell grandfather.

passage:
"You're alive, then," Irawati said, when Asif finally came to the bus stop on Monday morning.
"Ira, listen—"
"Six messages. Saturday was my science fair, Asif. You promised you'd come. Not even a thumbs up."
"I know, I—"
"No, it's fine. I get it now. You just don't care about my stuff. Everyone said you're like that."
Asif pulled his phone out and held it up. The screen was cracked across, dark. "It fell when we were rushing out on Friday night. My Nani was taken to the hospital. I was there all weekend. I didn't have anyone's number written down."
Irawati stared at the cracked screen. "Is she... okay?"
"She's home now. Resting."
"I thought..." Irawati stopped. She had spent two days deciding who he was, and not one minute wondering where he was.
"I'm sorry," she said. "Tell me about Nani?"

qa.q: What had Irawati sent Asif over the weekend?
qa.a: She had sent six messages.

qa.q: Why did 'you just don't care' feel like the obvious explanation to Irawati?
qa.a: She was hurt that he missed her science fair, and without any other information his silence seemed to show what kind of friend he was, especially as others had said he was like that.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation, and what did Irawati choose to do?
qa.a: When Asif held up the cracked phone and explained about his Nani, Irawati saw she had judged him without wondering what was happening, and she apologised and asked about Nani.

qa.q: What was the weekend like from Asif's side?
qa.a: For Asif it was a frightening weekend at the hospital with a broken phone and no numbers written down, and then he was accused of not caring the moment he arrived.

grounding: It shows a teenager assuming a friend's silence meant he did not care, never thinking of a broken phone or a family emergency.

passage:
Last month, before my dance recital, I was so sure I knew what kind of friend Payal was. I'm Indu, and I'm fifteen. Payal had promised to sit in the front row. The chair I'd saved for her stayed empty. Afterwards I sent her a long message, all capitals at the end, and she didn't reply for three days.
In those three days I decided everything. She was jealous. She only cared about her new friends. I even told my cousin that Payal "was always a bit selfish."
Then her reply came: her family had moved house that week, the internet at the new flat wasn't working, and her phone had gone in a box that got lost in the shifting. She'd only just found it.
What bothers me now is how quickly I built a whole person out of one empty chair, and how I never once thought of a move, a box or a dead connection.

qa.q: How long did Payal take to reply to Indu's message?
qa.a: She didn't reply for three days.

qa.q: Why did deciding that Payal was jealous feel so reasonable to Indu at the time?
qa.a: Indu was hurt by the empty chair, and with no reply, explaining it by Payal's character felt more certain than imagining things Indu could not see.

qa.q: If Indu faced another silence like this, what could Indu try before deciding?
qa.a: Indu could list a few everyday reasons a friend might go quiet, like a move or a broken phone, and wait or ask gently before telling anyone what the friend is like.

qa.q: How might Payal feel when she finally reads the long message ending in capitals?
qa.a: Payal would probably feel sad and a little defensive, having missed the recital because of a chaotic move, and then finding herself judged for it.

grounding: It shows a teenager deciding a friend who did not reply was uncaring, without thinking of circumstances such as a move or a lost phone.

passage:
Vaibhav,
I'm writing this because you clearly don't read messages. I sent you eleven texts yesterday about the dance audition. Eleven. You saw them, I'm sure, and you didn't reply to one. On my big day. I thought we were friends, but I guess you only care when you need notes before exams. Chitra said you were probably busy with cricket. Busy for a whole day? No. You just don't care about anyone except yourself, and I'm done pretending you do.

Kavitha
PS. Your mum called my mum this morning, something about your Nani and the hospital. I didn't listen properly. Doesn't change anything.

passage: Ritu, I'm telling you, Farah is the worst. We planned to go to the book fair at four, right? I waited at the gate for forty minutes. Forty! I messaged her six times, called her twice. Nothing. Not even a sorry. This is just who she is. She did the same thing in Class 7 when she forgot my birthday. She thinks her time matters more than everyone else's. What? No, her phone was fine yesterday. Why would it suddenly... okay, it's old, fine, it dies sometimes. But she could have borrowed someone's. Unless she wasn't near anyone. Or... no. Look, Preeti knows people, and Farah just doesn't care. Why are you shaking your head?

qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.a: Preeti feels hurt and annoyed after waiting, so the silence feels like proof of Farah's character, and the old phone that dies seems like an excuse.

passage:
Thursday. Leela sent Kishore the photos from the science exhibition: their project, their prize. Blue ticks. No reply. By night she had typed, "wow ok thanks for caring," and sent it.
Friday. Kishore wasn't in school. Leela told the group, "He's probably sulking because I got the stage for the prize." Someone laughed. She felt clever, and a little sick.
Sunday. Kishore's cousin posted in the class group: Kishore's father had been in a road accident on Thursday evening; he was stable now, and Kishore had been at the hospital for three days. Leela read it standing in the kitchen. She scrolled up to her own message, "thanks for caring," and her hand went cold. Then she typed, slowly, "I'm so sorry. I didn't know. Can I bring you food?"

qa.q: Where had Kishore been for three days?
qa.a: At the hospital, after his father's road accident.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she read the cousin's post?
qa.a: She felt shocked and ashamed, her hand going cold as she saw how wrong her message had been.

qa.q: What did Leela do right on Sunday, and what could she have done on Thursday?
qa.a: She apologised and offered food; on Thursday she could have asked if Kishore was okay instead of assuming he didn't care.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel seeing "thanks for caring" among his messages?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and too tired to explain, having spent three days at the hospital with his father.

grounding: Over a few days, a teenager decides a friend's silence means he doesn't care, then learns of a family emergency.

passage: Devika, you've been checking that phone every two minutes. Your friend hasn't replied, and you've decided she doesn't care? Listen to your Hafsa Khala. When I was in Class 11, we had no phones, only letters and one landline in the lane. I wrote my best friend a long letter about a boy I liked, and a fight with my Abbu. Two weeks, no reply. Then she didn't come to my birthday. I told everyone she was selfish, that she had new friends now. I even tore up her photo. A month later her younger brother came to our door. Their mother had been in hospital all that time, and my friend was cooking, cleaning, sitting by the bed. My letter was still unopened on her table. I never forgot how quickly I decided who she was.

qa.q: What did Hafsa Khala tear up?
qa.a: Her friend's photo.

qa.q: What was young Hafsa feeling when her friend missed her birthday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry, and decided her friend was selfish and had new friends, without imagining what else might be happening.

qa.q: Which moment in the story could Hafsa have handled differently?
qa.a: When the letter went unanswered, she could have asked the friend's family if all was well instead of telling everyone her friend was selfish.

qa.q: What was that month like for the friend?
qa.a: The friend was busy cooking, cleaning and sitting by her mother's hospital bed, with no time even to open a letter.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding a friend who did not reply was uncaring when the friend was really caught up in a family crisis.

passage: 11:05 p.m., the night before the chemistry exam. Kalyani had sent Rajni four messages asking for the photos of the organic notes. Two grey ticks, never blue. "Wow," Kalyani muttered. "She's online all day, but for me, nothing." She had no notes for three chapters and less than eight hours before the exam. She wrote a fifth message and deleted it, then wrote, "Thanks for nothing." Her finger shook over send. Instead she tried the class group, and a boy she barely knew sent the photos at midnight. In the morning, at the school gate, Rajni ran up, hair wet, eyes red. "Our whole building had no power last night. My phone died at nine. I charged it in the bus just now and saw your messages." Kalyani felt her face go hot. The deleted message was still in her head.

qa.q: How many messages had Kalyani sent Rajni by 11:05 p.m.?
qa.a: Four messages asking for the photos of the organic notes.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she typed "Thanks for nothing"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry, sure that Rajni was ignoring her on purpose while being online all day.

qa.q: What helped Kalyani avoid making things worse, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: Not sending the message and asking the class group helped; next time she could think of dead phones or power cuts before deciding a friend doesn't care.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt if the "Thanks for nothing" message had been waiting for her?
qa.a: Rajni would likely have felt hurt and unfairly accused, since her phone had died in a power cut.

grounding: Shows a teenager, under exam pressure, deciding a friend who did not reply is uncaring when the friend's phone had simply died.

passage: Vikas saw Tanvir coming out of the stationery shop near the Sector 15 market and waved hard. Tanvir looked straight through him and walked on, fast, head down. Vikas felt his cheeks burn. They had sat together all year. That evening he told his cousin, "Tanvir's become so full of himself since he made the football team. Didn't even say hi." He left Tanvir out of the group chat plan for Sunday's movie. On Monday Tanvir wasn't in school. On Tuesday he came in quiet and pale, and at lunch he said, "Sorry about Saturday. I'd just got a call that my Nani had collapsed. I was running to the auto stand." Vikas stared at his lunchbox. He had built a whole story about Tanvir from one walk past.

qa.a: Coming out of the stationery shop near the Sector 15 market.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when Tanvir walked past without a word?
qa.a: Vikas felt embarrassed and snubbed, his cheeks burning, and quickly decided Tanvir had become full of himself.

qa.q: What could Vikas do before judging a friend who seems rude?

passage:
"Ujjwal, Ria still hasn't replied. Three hours!"

"Maybe she's busy, Trisha."

"No. She saw my message about the project. She just doesn't care."

"Did it say 'seen'?"

"...No, it's one tick."

"One tick means it didn't even reach her phone."

"She could have charged her phone."

"Maybe she's somewhere without charging."

"You always defend her."

"I'm not defending. I'm just saying we don't know."

The phone buzzed. Ria: "So sorry!! My Nani was taken to hospital this morning. Phone died at the hospital. Just saw your message."

Trisha stared at the screen. Her face went hot. "I called her uncaring."

"You didn't know."

"I didn't even think of anything else." Trisha typed quickly: "Don't worry about the project at all. Is your Nani okay? 🤍"

qa.a: Three hours!

qa.q: What did Trisha feel when Ria's message came?
qa.a: Trisha felt embarrassed and guilty, realising she had called Ria uncaring without thinking of other reasons.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal help Trisha think more fairly?

qa.q: How might Ria have felt if Trisha had sent an angry message?
qa.a: Ria would likely have felt hurt and more stressed while already worried about her Nani.

grounding: A teenager assumes a friend who didn't reply is uncaring, never thinking of a dead phone or family crisis.

passage:
I'm Damini. Last term, I was so angry with Arohi.

She didn't come to my birthday. She didn't reply to my messages for four days. When she came back to school, she was quiet and didn't even say sorry. I told everyone she was selfish. I thought, that's just who she is.

A week later, our class teacher mentioned that Arohi's family had been moving house suddenly. Her father's job had changed cities. They'd packed in three days. She'd been sleeping on boxes.

I felt awful. I had decided she was selfish without even wondering if something was wrong.

I went to find her at lunch. I said sorry. She said, "I wanted to tell you, but everything was so messy."

Now when someone goes quiet, I try to remember Arohi's boxes. There's usually a reason I can't see.

qa.q: How many days did Arohi not reply to Damini's messages?
qa.a: She didn't reply to my messages for four days.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after learning about Arohi's move?
qa.a: Damini felt awful and ashamed for deciding Arohi was selfish without wondering if something was wrong.

qa.q: What does Damini now try to remember, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Damini remembers Arohi's boxes, a reminder that there's usually a hidden reason when someone goes quiet.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when classmates called her selfish?
qa.a: Arohi probably felt hurt and alone, already stressed by the sudden move.

grounding: A teenager decides a friend is selfish for not replying, never thinking of a family crisis, until the truth comes out.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10

Kishore came to me today upset that his friend Pratik "ignored" him in the corridor and hasn't replied to messages since Monday. Kishore said, "He's become arrogant since he got into the cricket team."

I asked Kishore whether he had noticed anything else about Pratik this week. He thought, and said Pratik had been absent on Tuesday, and looked tired.

I couldn't share private details, but I knew Pratik's family was going through a difficult time. I told Kishore gently that there might be things happening for Pratik that we can't see, and that people who seem rude are sometimes just overwhelmed.

Kishore was quiet. Then he said, "I didn't even think of that. I just thought he'd changed."

He's decided to send Pratik a message asking if he's okay, instead of an angry one.

Tenzin

qa.q: Since when has Pratik not replied to Kishore's messages?
qa.a: Since Monday.

qa.q: Why did Kishore think Pratik had become arrogant?
qa.a: Kishore felt hurt at being ignored, and explained it by Pratik's character rather than any situation he couldn't see.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that helped without breaking privacy?
qa.a: Tenzin asked what else Kishore had noticed and gently suggested unseen pressures, without sharing Pratik's private details.

qa.q: How might Pratik feel receiving a message asking if he's okay?
qa.a: Pratik might feel relieved and cared for during a difficult time.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager who assumes a quiet friend has become arrogant, never thinking of a family crisis.
